---
title: "Neural networks"
---

Neural networks make predictions by passing inputs through a sequence of
linear transformations and activation functions. The first notebook traces
that calculation with a small gas-turbine example before introducing how a
network learns its weights.

## 1. Forward propagation

Follow a mini-batch of gas-turbine operating observations, using all nine
measured operating features, through a neural network with one hidden layer.
Inspect the shape of every array, compare ReLU with the identity activation,
and count the model parameters.

[View the notebook](01-forward-propagation.ipynb)

Use a small $2 \rightarrow 3 \rightarrow 1$ network to edit the two inputs,
every weight, and every bias. See how these choices define a probability field
and produce a forward-pass prediction.

[Explore forward propagation](02-forward-propagation-explorer.qmd)

## 2. Backpropagation

Trace how a prediction error produces gradients for every parameter in the
same small network. Follow one selected observation through the chain rule,
then watch the full-dataset gradient update the model.

[Explore backpropagation](03-backpropagation-explorer.qmd)

## 3. Convolutional neural networks

### 3.1 Convolution fundamentals

Build intuition for convolution before introducing a trainable neural network.
Start with a sliding filter on a one-dimensional signal, then apply
hand-designed filters to a two-dimensional image to see feature maps and
weight sharing.

[Work through the notebook](03-convolution-basics.ipynb)

### 3.2 CNN on MNIST

Use MNIST to build a first end-to-end PyTorch CNN: image tensors,
mini-batches, convolutional layers, training, and error analysis.

[Work through the notebook](04-mnist-cnn.ipynb)

### 3.3 CNN for steel-surface inspection

Reuse the same workflow for the six-class NEU-CLS steel-surface defect task.
Build a custom dataset, train a compact CNN, and inspect held-out errors.

[Work through the notebook](05-neu-cls-cnn.ipynb)
